$$a^3+b^3=10^3-3\cdot21\cdot10$$

$$a^3+b^3=1000-630$$

$$a^3+b^3=370$$

The claim asserts $371$, but the identity produces $370$.

Since $370\ne371$, the claim does not hold.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The unordered pair $\{a,b\}$ is exactly the root set of the monic quadratic with those coefficients.

Form the monic quadratic with sum $a+b$ and product $ab$:

$$t^2-(a+b)t+ab=0$$

$$t^2-10t+21=0$$

Factor the left-hand side:

$$t^2-10t+21=(t-3)(t-7)$$

The roots are therefore $t=3$ and $t=7$, so

$$\{a,b\}=\{3,7\}$$

That matches the claimed unordered pair.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Sum of reciprocals is the elementary quotient of sum by product.

$$\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{a+b}{ab}$$

Substitute $a+b=10$ and $ab=21$:

$$\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{10}{21}$$

The claim asserts $\dfrac{21}{10}$. Since $\dfrac{10}{21}\neq\dfrac{21}{10}$, the claim does not hold.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only the elementary symmetric data $a+b=10$ and $ab=21$ are recorded. Every claim must follow from those two numbers (or from the monic quadratic $t^{2}-10t+21=0$ whose roots are $a$ and $b$).

The standing identities are

$$a^{2}+b^{2}=(a+b)^{2}-2ab$$

$$(a-b)^{2}=(a+b)^{2}-4ab$$

$$a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)^{3}-3ab(a+b)$$

$$\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{a+b}{ab}$$

Substituting the archive values recovers $a^{2}+b^{2}=58$, $(a-b)^{2}=16$, $a^{3}+b^{3}=370$, and $\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{10}{21}$. Factoring $t^{2}-10t+21=(t-3)(t-7)$ shows $\{a,b\}=\{3,7\}$.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 12
tasks.context: A symbolic calculator studies $R(x)=\dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ and $S(x)=\dfrac1{x-2}+\dfrac1{x+2}$. The first expression is defined for $x\ne 2$, while the second also excludes $x=-2$. Simplifications must retain these original domain restrictions even after factors cancel.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On the domain $x\ne2$, factor the difference of squares in the numerator and cancel the shared linear factor.

Factor first:

$$x^{2}-4=(x-2)(x+2)$$

Divide by the remaining linear factor:

$$R(x)=\dfrac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}$$

$$R(x)=x+2\qquad(x\ne2)$$

The simplified form is exactly $x+2$ on the domain.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The expression $R(x)$ is undefined at the excluded point $x=2$, so the value $R(2)$ is not defined by the formula.

Substitute the forbidden input into the original fraction:

$$R(2)=\dfrac{2^{2}-4}{2-2}$$

$$=\dfrac{0}{0}$$

The denominator vanishes, so $R$ has no finite value at that point.

The claim asserts $R(2)=4$, which would require evaluating past a hole in the domain.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Combine the two reciprocals over the common denominator $(x-2)(x+2)$.

$$S(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}+\dfrac{1}{x+2}$$

$$=\dfrac{(x+2)+(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+2)}$$

$$=\dfrac{2x}{x^2-4}\qquad(x\neq\pm2)$$

That matches the claimed simplified form.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

On the domain $x\neq\pm2$, combine the reciprocals in $S$ and evaluate at the admissible point $x=0$.

Recover the single-fraction form:

$$S(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}+\dfrac{1}{x+2}=\dfrac{2x}{x^2-4}\qquad(x\neq\pm2)$$

Substitute $x=0$:

$$S(0)=\dfrac{2\cdot0}{0^2-4}$$

$$=\dfrac{0}{-4}$$

$$=0$$

Since $0\neq\pm2$, the point is in the domain, and the value equals the claimed $0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Solve $S(x)=0$ on the domain $x\ne\pm2$.

Using the recovered form:

$$\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}-4}=0$$

A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero and the denominator is not:

$$2x=0\Longrightarrow x=0$$

And $0\ne\pm2$, so $x=0$ is admissible.

No other numerator root exists, so there is exactly one real solution.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Work on the stated domains: $R$ excludes $x=2$, and $S$ excludes $x=\pm2$. Factor and cancel before evaluating, and combine the two reciprocals in $S$ over a common denominator.

$$R(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}=\dfrac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=x+2\quad(x\ne2)$$

$$S(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}+\dfrac{1}{x+2}=\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}-4}\quad(x\ne\pm2)$$

In particular $S(0)=0$, and $S(x)=0$ forces $x=0$ on the domain.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 13
tasks.context: A materials model fixes a positive scale variable at $x=16$. The report uses the principal real roots and the exponent laws $x^r x^s=x^{r+s}$ and $(x^r)^s=x^{rs}$. Negative exponents are interpreted as reciprocals, and all claims refer to this same positive value of $x$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The materials model fixes the positive scale at $x=16$. The principal square root is the unique nonnegative number whose square is $16$.

Compute:

$$x^{1/2}=\sqrt{16}$$

$$4^2=16$$

$$x^{1/2}=4$$

The claim asserts $x^{1/2}=4$, which matches the principal root of the fixed scale $x=16$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

With the fixed scale $x=16$, the principal fourth root is the positive square root of the principal square root.

Chain the root laws:

$$x^{1/4}=(x^{1/2})^{1/2}$$

$$x^{1/2}=\sqrt{16}$$

$$=4$$

$$x^{1/4}=4^{1/2}$$

$$=2$$

Check: $2^4=16$. The claim $x^{1/4}=2$ matches.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A negative exponent means the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power, at the fixed scale $x=16$.

First take the principal square root:

$$x^{1/2}=\sqrt{16}$$

$$=4$$

Then invert:

$$x^{-1/2}=\dfrac{1}{x^{1/2}}$$

$$=\dfrac{1}{4}$$

The claim asserts $x^{-1/2}=\dfrac{1}{4}$, which matches the reciprocal of $4$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Rewrite the fractional power $x^{3/4}$ as a cube of the fourth root, using the fixed scale $x=16$.

From the fourth-root evaluation:

$$x^{1/4}=2$$

Raise to the third power:

$$x^{3/4}=(x^{1/4})^3$$

$$=2^3$$

$$=8$$

Alternatively, $x^{3/4}=(x^{1/2})\cdot(x^{1/4})=4\cdot2=8$. The claim $x^{3/4}=8$ matches.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Any nonzero real number to the power $0$ equals $1$, not $0$. The scale is fixed at $x=16\neq0$.

By the zero-exponent rule:

$$x^{0}=1\qquad(x=16\neq0)$$

Compare with the claim $x^{0}=0$:

$$1\neq0$$

Numeric check: $16^{0}=1$. The asserted value $0$ is wrong.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The scale is fixed at the positive value $x=16$. Principal real roots and the exponent laws $x^{r}x^{s}=x^{r+s}$ and $(x^{r})^{s}=x^{rs}$ are in force; negative exponents mean reciprocals.

$$x^{1/2}=4,\qquad x^{1/4}=2,\qquad x^{-1/2}=\dfrac{1}{4},\qquad x^{3/4}=8$$

Also $x^{0}=1$ for this nonzero $x$.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 14
tasks.context: A calibration reading $x$ is accepted when its distance from the target 4 is at most 3 units, written $|x-4|\le 3$. A warning band uses the strict version $|x-4|<3$. The endpoint readings are physically possible and all readings are real.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Translate the closed distance inequality $|x-4|\le3$ into a closed interval about the target $4$.

Unfold:

$$|x-4|\le3\Longleftrightarrow-3\le x-4\le3$$

Add $4$ through the chain:

$$1\le x\le7$$

That is the closed interval $[1,7]$. Endpoints: $|1-4|=3\le3$ and $|7-4|=3\le3$, both accepted. The claim matches.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A closed acceptance interval includes each finite endpoint, so test the inequality there.

An endpoint of the closed acceptance interval is included.

Check the acceptance inequality at $x=1$:

$$| 1-4 |=|-3|$$

$$=3$$

$$|1-4|\le3$$

The inequality holds, so $x=1$ is accepted.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The warning band is the strict inequality $|x-4|<3$, so endpoints of the acceptance interval are excluded.

At the right endpoint $x=7$:

$$|7-4|=3$$

The warning test requires $|x-4|<3$, but

$$3\nless3$$

Hence $x=7$ fails the strict test. It is accepted ($|7-4|\le3$) but not in the warning band.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Count the integers lying in the closed acceptance interval $[1,7]$ coming from $|x-4|\le3$.

The integers from $1$ through $7$ are

$$1,2,3,4,5,6,7$$

The inclusive count is

$$7-1+1=7$$

There are exactly $7$ accepted integer readings, matching the claim.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The complementary region is outside the closed interval, not inside the open middle.

By definition,

$$|x-4|>3\Longleftrightarrow\bigl(x<1\bigr)\lor\bigl(x>7\bigr)$$

The claim instead writes $1<x<7$, which is the warning band $|x-4|<3$.

Those two regions are disjoint.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Distance from the target $4$ is measured by $|x-4|$. The acceptance rule $|x-4|\le3$ is the closed interval $[1,7]$, while the warning band $|x-4|<3$ is the open interval $(1,7)$.

Endpoints $x=1$ and $x=7$ are accepted but not in the warning band. There are $7$ integers in $[1,7]$. The complementary inequality $|x-4|>3$ is $x<1$ or $x>7$, not the open middle interval.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 15
tasks.context: An algebra archive stores two real numbers $a$ and $b$ only through the records $a+b=9$ and $ab=20$. The original order was not recorded, so every conclusion must follow from symmetric identities or from the quadratic having roots $a$ and $b$. No decimal approximation is used in the audit.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 17

Compare with the claim $x^{0}=0$:

$$1\neq0$$

Numeric check: $81^{0}=1$. The asserted value $0$ is wrong.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The scale is fixed at the positive value $x=81$. Principal real roots and the exponent laws $x^{r}x^{s}=x^{r+s}$ and $(x^{r})^{s}=x^{rs}$ are in force; negative exponents mean reciprocals.

$$x^{1/2}=9,\qquad x^{1/4}=3,\qquad x^{-1/2}=\dfrac{1}{9},\qquad x^{3/4}=27$$

Also $x^{0}=1$ for this nonzero $x$.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 18
tasks.context: A calibration reading $x$ is accepted when its distance from the target 5 is at most 3 units, written $|x-5|\le 3$. A warning band uses the strict version $|x-5|<3$. The endpoint readings are physically possible and all readings are real.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Translate the closed distance inequality $|x-5|\le3$ into a closed interval about the target $5$.

Unfold:

$$|x-5|\le3\Longleftrightarrow-3\le x-5\le3$$

Add $5$ through the chain:

$$2\le x\le8$$

That is the closed interval $[2,8]$. Endpoints: $|2-5|=3\le3$ and $|8-5|=3\le3$, both accepted. The claim matches.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A closed acceptance interval includes each finite endpoint, so test the inequality there.

An endpoint of the closed acceptance interval is included.

Check the acceptance inequality at $x=2$:

$$| 2-5 |=|-3|$$

$$=3$$

$$|2-5|\le3$$

The inequality holds, so $x=2$ is accepted.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The warning band is the strict inequality $|x-5|<3$, so endpoints of the acceptance interval are excluded.

At the right endpoint $x=8$:

$$|8-5|=3$$

The warning test requires $|x-5|<3$, but

$$3\nless3$$

Hence $x=8$ fails the strict test. It is accepted ($|8-5|\le3$) but not in the warning band.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Count the integers lying in the closed acceptance interval $[2,8]$ coming from $|x-5|\le3$.

The integers from $2$ through $8$ are

$$2,3,4,5,6,7,8$$

The inclusive count is

$$8-2+1=7$$

There are exactly $7$ accepted integer readings, matching the claim.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The complementary region is outside the closed interval, not inside the open middle.

By definition,

$$|x-5|>3\Longleftrightarrow\bigl(x<2\bigr)\lor\bigl(x>8\bigr)$$

The claim instead writes $2<x<8$, which is the warning band $|x-5|<3$.

Those two regions are disjoint.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Distance from the target $5$ is measured by $|x-5|$. The acceptance rule $|x-5|\le3$ is the closed interval $[2,8]$, while the warning band $|x-5|<3$ is the open interval $(2,8)$.

Endpoints $x=2$ and $x=8$ are accepted but not in the warning band. There are $7$ integers in $[2,8]$. The complementary inequality $|x-5|>3$ is $x<2$ or $x>8$, not the open middle interval.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 19
tasks.context: An algebra archive stores two real numbers $a$ and $b$ only through the records $a+b=11$ and $ab=18$. The original order was not recorded, so every conclusion must follow from symmetric identities or from the quadratic having roots $a$ and $b$. No decimal approximation is used in the audit.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Sum of squares follows from the square of the sum after the mixed product is peeled off.

Start from the square of the recorded sum:

Rearrange to isolate the sum of squares:

$$a^2+b^2=(a+b)^2-2ab$$

Substitute $a+b=11$ and $ab=18$:

$$a^2+b^2=11^2-2\cdot18$$

$$a^2+b^2=121-36$$

$$a^2+b^2=85$$

The claim asserts the same value $85$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The squared gap $(a-b)^{2}$ is another elementary identity in $a+b$ and $ab$.

Expand $(a-b)^{2}$ and rewrite in elementary symmetric form:

$$(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2$$

$$(a-b)^2=(a+b)^2-4ab$$

Substitute the archive values:

$$(a-b)^2=11^2-4\cdot18$$

$$(a-b)^2=121-72$$

$$(a-b)^2=49$$

The claim is $(a-b)^2=49$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Cubes expand through the same sum and product; the middle term is $3ab(a+b)$.

The cube-sum identity reads

$$a^3+b^3=(a+b)^3-3ab(a+b)$$

Substitute $a+b=11$ and $ab=18$:

$$a^3+b^3=11^3-3\cdot18\cdot11$$

$$a^3+b^3=1331-594$$

$$a^3+b^3=737$$

The claim asserts $738$, but the identity produces $737$.

Since $737\ne738$, the claim does not hold.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The unordered pair $\{a,b\}$ is exactly the root set of the monic quadratic with those coefficients.

Form the monic quadratic with sum $a+b$ and product $ab$:

$$t^2-(a+b)t+ab=0$$

$$t^2-11t+18=0$$

Factor the left-hand side:

$$t^2-11t+18=(t-2)(t-9)$$

The roots are therefore $t=2$ and $t=9$, so

$$\{a,b\}=\{2,9\}$$

That matches the claimed unordered pair.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Sum of reciprocals is the elementary quotient of sum by product.

$$\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{a+b}{ab}$$

Substitute $a+b=11$ and $ab=18$:

$$\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{11}{18}$$

The claim asserts $\dfrac{18}{11}$. Since $\dfrac{11}{18}\neq\dfrac{18}{11}$, the claim does not hold.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only the elementary symmetric data $a+b=11$ and $ab=18$ are recorded. Every claim must follow from those two numbers (or from the monic quadratic $t^{2}-11t+18=0$ whose roots are $a$ and $b$).

The standing identities are

$$a^{2}+b^{2}=(a+b)^{2}-2ab$$

$$(a-b)^{2}=(a+b)^{2}-4ab$$

$$a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)^{3}-3ab(a+b)$$

$$\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{a+b}{ab}$$

Substituting the archive values recovers $a^{2}+b^{2}=85$, $(a-b)^{2}=49$, $a^{3}+b^{3}=737$, and $\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{11}{18}$. Factoring $t^{2}-11t+18=(t-2)(t-9)$ shows $\{a,b\}=\{2,9\}$.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 20
tasks.context: A symbolic calculator studies $R(x)=\dfrac{x^2-16}{x-4}$ and $S(x)=\dfrac1{x-4}+\dfrac1{x+4}$. The first expression is defined for $x\ne 4$, while the second also excludes $x=-4$. Simplifications must retain these original domain restrictions even after factors cancel.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On the domain $x\ne4$, factor the difference of squares in the numerator and cancel the shared linear factor.

Factor first:

$$x^{2}-16=(x-4)(x+4)$$

Divide by the remaining linear factor:

$$R(x)=\dfrac{(x-4)(x+4)}{x-4}$$

$$R(x)=x+4\qquad(x\ne4)$$

The simplified form is exactly $x+4$ on the domain.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The expression $R(x)$ is undefined at the excluded point $x=4$, so the value $R(4)$ is not defined by the formula.

Substitute the forbidden input into the original fraction:

$$R(4)=\dfrac{4^{2}-16}{4-4}$$

$$=\dfrac{0}{0}$$

The denominator vanishes, so $R$ has no finite value at that point.

The claim asserts $R(4)=8$, which would require evaluating past a hole in the domain.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Combine the two reciprocals over the common denominator $(x-4)(x+4)$.

$$S(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-4}+\dfrac{1}{x+4}$$

$$=\dfrac{(x+4)+(x-4)}{(x-4)(x+4)}$$

$$=\dfrac{2x}{x^2-16}\qquad(x\neq\pm4)$$

That matches the claimed simplified form.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

On the domain $x\neq\pm4$, combine the reciprocals in $S$ and evaluate at the admissible point $x=0$.

Recover the single-fraction form:

$$S(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-4}+\dfrac{1}{x+4}=\dfrac{2x}{x^2-16}\qquad(x\neq\pm4)$$

Substitute $x=0$:

$$S(0)=\dfrac{2\cdot0}{0^2-16}$$

$$=\dfrac{0}{-16}$$

$$=0$$

Since $0\neq\pm4$, the point is in the domain, and the value equals the claimed $0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Solve $S(x)=0$ on the domain $x\ne\pm4$.

Using the recovered form:

$$\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}-16}=0$$

A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero and the denominator is not:

$$2x=0\Longrightarrow x=0$$

And $0\ne\pm4$, so $x=0$ is admissible.

No other numerator root exists, so there is exactly one real solution.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Work on the stated domains: $R$ excludes $x=4$, and $S$ excludes $x=\pm4$. Factor and cancel before evaluating, and combine the two reciprocals in $S$ over a common denominator.

$$R(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-16}{x-4}=\dfrac{(x-4)(x+4)}{x-4}=x+4\quad(x\ne4)$$

$$S(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-4}+\dfrac{1}{x+4}=\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}-16}\quad(x\ne\pm4)$$

In particular $S(0)=0$, and $S(x)=0$ forces $x=0$ on the domain.
